warmup.q: You traceroute a card issuer's API. Hop 4 prints * * *, and hops 5 to 9 answer normally. What does hop 4's line tell you?
options: Hop 4 drops your packets, so it is the likely cause of your slow API calls
Hop 4 forwards packets fine but sends no ICMP answers to you, so its line tells you almost nothing
The path is broken at hop 4, and hops 5 to 9 were remembered from an earlier run
Hop 4 is a switch, which has no IP address to show
warmup.why: The probes for hops 5 to 9 passed through hop 4, so it forwards them. Its * * * only means no Time Exceeded came back from it: it filters ICMP, or it rate-limits its replies. Blaming hop 4 is the tempting mistake, because a star looks like loss. Switches are invisible to traceroute for a different reason: they never touch the TTL, so they never appear as a hop at all.

sections.h: Every router asks one question per packet: which route matches best
sections.html:
A packet from client (10.10.1.10) to ledger (10.10.4.40) in the lab network crosses three links and two routers: client to router over lan, router to router2 over a link called tunnel, router2 to ledger over dc. Nobody on the way knows the whole path. Each router looks only at the destination address, picks the next machine to hand the packet to, and forgets it. That hand-off is called forwarding, and the next machine is the next hop.

The router makes that choice from its routing table: a list of address blocks, each with a way out. Start with the simplest table that could work, one line that says "everything goes to my gateway". That is the default route, 0.0.0.0/0, and lesson 3 of this track showed it on client. It is enough for a host with one way out.

It is not enough for router. Router has three cards, on lan, wan and tunnel. A packet for 10.10.2.20 must leave on wan, one for 10.10.4.40 must go into the tunnel to router2, and one for the internet must go to Docker's gateway. So a router keeps one line per block it knows about. The kernel adds a line for each card's own subnet when the card gets its address (10.10.2.0/24 dev eth0, a connected route). People add static routes by hand (ip route add 10.10.4.0/24 via 10.10.3.3). The default route catches the rest.

Now the lines overlap. In the Try it below you give client one line for all the lab's networks, 10.10.0.0/16 via 10.10.1.2. Client already has 10.10.1.0/24 dev eth0 and the default. A packet for 10.10.1.20 (peer) matches all three. The rule is the one from lesson 3: longest prefix match. Of all matching lines, the one with the most network bits wins, because it knows the destination most precisely. /24 beats /16 beats /0, so peer is still reached directly on the link, while ledger goes to router. The rule lets you write a broad line plus narrow exceptions, and the order of the lines never matters.

Where do routes come from on the internet? Nobody types them in. Routers tell each other which blocks they can reach, with routing protocols: OSPF inside one company's network, and BGP between networks, where an internet provider announces "send 104.20.0.0/16 to me". A full BGP table holds around a million IPv4 prefixes. The question per packet stays the same, and routers answer it in hardware.

One property matters for everything that follows. Each router decides alone, with no memory of where the packet has been. That lets the internet route around a broken link. It also means two routers with inconsistent tables can pass a packet back and forth forever, which is the next section.

try.title: Add a route and ask the kernel which line wins
steps: From the labs folder, start the lab network: docker compose -f env/net.yml up -d. It now has a second router: router2 joins router to a network called dc through a link called tunnel (MTU 1400), and ledger (10.10.4.40) sits on dc. The comment at the top of env/net.yml draws the whole thing.

Give client one route for every lab network, then ask the kernel how it would send to three addresses. Predict first: straight onto the link, via router (10.10.1.2), or via Docker's gateway (10.10.1.1)?
Last, ask router how it would reach ledger. Router has no route for dc yet. Predict where its default route sends the packet. Leave it that way: the traceroute Try it uses this mistake.
On a Mac, netstat -rn -f inet prints the routing table and route -n get 10.10.4.40 asks the same question as ip route get.

code.title: in labs/
code.html: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ip route add 10.10.0.0/16 via 10.10.1.2 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ip route docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ip route get 10.10.1.20 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ip route get 10.10.4.40 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ip route get 1.1.1.1 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec router ip route get 10.10.4.40

try.expect:
From one run:

default via 10.10.1.1 dev eth0
10.10.0.0/16 via 10.10.1.2 dev eth0
10.10.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.10.1.10
10.10.2.0/24 via 10.10.1.2 dev eth0
10.10.1.20 dev eth0 src 10.10.1.10 uid 0
    cache
10.10.4.40 via 10.10.1.2 dev eth0 src 10.10.1.10 uid 0
    cache
1.1.1.1 via 10.10.1.1 dev eth0 src 10.10.1.10 uid 0
    cache
10.10.4.40 via 10.10.1.1 dev eth1 src 10.10.1.2 uid 0
    cache

10.10.1.20 matches all of /0, /16 and /24, and the /24 wins, so there is no via: client still reaches peer directly. 10.10.4.40 matches /16 and /0, and /16 wins. 1.1.1.1 matches only the default. Router has no line for 10.10.4.0/24, so its default route sends ledger's packets to Docker's gateway, which is wrong. The eth number on router may differ on your machine, because Docker numbers a container's cards in no fixed order.

sections.h: TTL stops a packet that would loop forever, and ICMP says why it died
sections.html:
Make two routers disagree. Router says 10.10.9.0/24 is behind router2, and router2 says it is behind router. A packet for 10.10.9.9 now bounces between them. Nothing in their tables says "stop", and every new packet joins the bounce, until the tunnel is full of copies of traffic that will never arrive. Real loops happen for a few seconds whenever a link fails and one router learns about it before its neighbour.

The fix is a counter in every IPv4 header: the TTL (time to live), the byte you met in lesson 1. The sender sets it, and Linux starts at 64. Every router lowers it by one before it forwards. A router that receives a packet with TTL 1 may not send it on, because it would arrive with 0, so it drops it. A looping packet now dies after at most 255 links. In the Try it below, a ping with TTL 64 crossed the tunnel 63 times in well under a millisecond and then died.

A silent drop leaves the sender guessing, so the router also sends a short report back to the packet's source. Those reports are ICMP, the Internet Control Message Protocol. ICMP rides inside IP with protocol number 1, the way TCP is 6 and UDP 17. This one is ICMP Time Exceeded, type 11. Every ICMP error quotes the start of the packet that died: its IP header plus at least the next 8 bytes (RFC 792), which is exactly enough for the UDP or TCP ports. The sender's kernel uses those ports to find the socket the error belongs to. Linux quotes more, up to 576 bytes in total.

These are the ICMP messages you will meet:

Type, code Name Sent when
8 and 0 echo request, echo reply ping asks, the host answers
11, 0 time exceeded a router dropped a packet whose TTL ran out
3, 0 net unreachable a router has no route for the destination
3, 3 port unreachable a UDP datagram arrived for a port nobody listens on
3, 4 fragmentation needed the next link is too small (the last section)

The router writes its own address as the source, and Linux picks the card on its route back to you. That is why the Try it shows the error coming from 10.10.3.3, router2's tunnel side.

Two rules stop ICMP from making a bad situation worse. Nobody sends an ICMP error about an ICMP error, or two confused routers could trade errors forever (RFC 1122). And routers rate-limit their errors: Linux sends time exceeded and unreachable messages to one destination at about one a second after a short burst (net.ipv4.icmp_ratelimit is 1000 ms). Many firewalls drop ICMP altogether. So a missing ICMP message is normal and proves nothing, which matters in the next section.

try.title: Build a routing loop and watch the TTL run out
steps: In one terminal, listen on router2: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec router2 tcpdump -i any -nn -v icmp. -v prints each packet's TTL.

In a second terminal, give router and router2 routes for 10.10.9.0/24 that point at each other, then send one ping with TTL 5 (-t 5). Predict first: how many times will router2 see the packet, with which TTLs, and who reports the death?
Send one more ping with the normal TTL of 64, and read who reports it this time. Then stop tcpdump with Ctrl-C and delete the two bad routes with the last two lines.

code.title: second terminal, in labs/
code.html: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec router ip route add 10.10.9.0/24 via 10.10.3.3 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec router2 ip route add 10.10.9.0/24 via 10.10.3.2 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ping -c 1 -t 5 10.10.9.9 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ping -c 1 10.10.9.9 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec router ip route del 10.10.9.0/24 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec router2 ip route del 10.10.9.0/24

try.expect:
The pings, from one run:

PING 10.10.9.9 (10.10.9.9) 56(84) bytes of data.
From 10.10.1.2 icmp_seq=1 Time to live exceeded

PING 10.10.9.9 (10.10.9.9) 56(84) bytes of data.
From 10.10.3.3 icmp_seq=1 Time to live exceeded

And router2's capture of the first one (timestamps and the second line of each packet trimmed):

eth1  In  IP (tos 0x0, ttl 4, id 55447, offset 0, flags [DF], proto ICMP (1), length 84)
eth1  Out IP (tos 0x0, ttl 3, id 55447, offset 0, flags [DF], proto ICMP (1), length 84)
eth1  In  IP (tos 0x0, ttl 2, id 55447, offset 0, flags [DF], proto ICMP (1), length 84)
eth1  Out IP (tos 0x0, ttl 1, id 55447, offset 0, flags [DF], proto ICMP (1), length 84)

The same packet (same id) arrives and leaves on the tunnel card twice, one TTL lower each time. Router gets it back with TTL 1 and reports it from 10.10.1.2, its lan address. With TTL 64 the packet crosses the tunnel 63 times and dies at router2, which reports from 10.10.3.3. That loop takes well under a millisecond, and tcpdump may miss some copies.

sections.h: Traceroute turns dying packets into a map of the path
sections.html:
In the late 1980s Van Jacobson turned the TTL rule into a tool. Send a probe with TTL 1: the first router drops it and tells you its address. Send TTL 2: the second router does. Keep going until the destination itself answers. That is traceroute, and nothing in it needs the routers' cooperation beyond the Time Exceeded they send anyway.

How does traceroute know it has arrived? Linux traceroute sends each probe as a UDP datagram to a high port nobody uses, 33434 for the first TTL and one more for each probe after it. When a probe finally reaches the destination, no program listens on that port, so the destination's kernel answers ICMP Port Unreachable. Time Exceeded means "one more hop"; Port Unreachable means "you are here". Traceroute matches each answer to its probe by the port in the quoted header, which also lets it send many probes at once (16 by default). It sends three probes per hop and prints the round trip time of each.

Step through the trace you are about to run, then read the stars.

A * means no answer came back for that probe within traceroute's wait. There are four common reasons. The router filters its ICMP, or its rate limit is used up for the moment. The probe really was lost. Or the answer had no way back. If later hops answer, the starred router forwarded the probe fine, and the star says nothing about loss. Stars from some hop to the very end mean the path breaks there, or that everything from there on filters ICMP, or that the destination's answers can't find their way home.

That last case is easy to miss. A reply needs a route too. In the lab network the server has no route back to lan, so its Port Unreachable messages never leave it, and the trace ends in stars, exactly like a dead host. A TCP connection to it fails the same way: the SYN arrives, and the SYN-ACK goes nowhere. The path back can also differ from the path there (asymmetric routing), and traceroute shows only the way there, while each round trip time it prints includes the way back.

Two variants help in practice. traceroute -T -p 443 sends TCP SYNs to port 443, which firewalls that allow web traffic let through. mtr repeats a traceroute every second and shows loss per hop; read its middle hops with the rate limit in mind, because a router that answers one probe in three still forwards everything.

stepper.title: Traceroute, one probe at a time
stepper.intro: client traces its path to ledger in the lab network, after the Try it in the first section added the routes. Each probe lives one hop longer than the last.

try.title: Trace the path, fix it, and trace again
steps: Trace from client to ledger with the router still missing its route for dc (from the first Try it). -n prints addresses without looking up names, -w 1 waits one second per probe and -m 5 stops after five hops. Predict hop 2.
Add the missing route on router and trace again.
Now trace the server, which has no route back to lan (lesson 3). Predict: will hop 2 show the server? Then give the server its way back and trace once more.
On a Mac, traceroute -n 1.1.1.1 works without sudo and shows your home router, your provider's routers and some stars.

sections.h: Every link has a size limit, and path MTU discovery finds the smallest
sections.html:
Lesson 2 of this track showed a host refusing to send 1,473 bytes of ping data over a link with a 1,500-byte MTU (maximum transmission unit, the largest packet a link carries). The host knew its own link's limit. It has no idea of the limits of links further away. In the lab network the tunnel between router and router2 carries at most 1,400 bytes, like a VPN link that wraps every packet in an extra header of its own.

So what should router do with a 1,500-byte packet for ledger? IPv4's first answer was fragmentation: the router cuts the packet into pieces that fit, and the destination glues them back together. It works and it is poor. Fragmenting costs the router work, losing one piece loses the whole packet, and firewalls and NATs can't see the ports in the later pieces. IPv6 routers never fragment at all (lesson 5).

The answer in use today is path MTU discovery (RFC 1191). The sender sets the Don't Fragment flag, and Linux does that for TCP and for ping. A router that can't forward a DF packet drops it and sends ICMP Destination Unreachable, Fragmentation Needed (type 3, code 4), with the next link's MTU written into the message. The sender lowers its packet size for that destination and remembers it: Linux keeps the learned value for 10 minutes, and ip route get shows it as mtu 1400. TCP sends the lost data again in smaller segments. The MSS from lesson 1 already covers the links at both ends, because each side announces one based on its own card. Path MTU discovery covers the links in between.

It has one weak point: it needs that ICMP message to arrive. Many firewalls drop every ICMP packet "for security". Then the sender never hears why its packets vanish. The TCP handshake and a small request pass, because they are small. The first full-size packet of the response vanishes, its retransmissions are just as big, and the connection hangs with no error at all. This is a PMTU black hole, and you will make one in the Try it.

The fixes, best first. Never block ICMP type 3 code 4: let it through every firewall, security group and network ACL on the path. On the router at the narrow link, clamp the MSS: the router rewrites the MSS in every passing SYN so that TCP never builds a segment too big for the tunnel (iptables -t mangle -A FORWARD -p tcp --tcp-flags SYN,RST SYN -j TCPMSS --clamp-mss-to-pmtu). Or let the transport find the size itself by probing with growing packets: packetization layer PMTUD (RFC 4821 for TCP, where Linux has it as net.ipv4.tcp_mtu_probing, and RFC 8899 for protocols on UDP such as QUIC). It doesn't need ICMP at all.

try.title: Make a PMTU black hole, then let ICMP through
steps: This needs routes from the earlier Try its (client's 10.10.0.0/16 and router's 10.10.4.0/24), and no big packets sent toward ledger yet: the kernel remembers a learned MTU for 10 minutes. If you have pinged ledger with big packets already, run docker compose -f env/net.yml restart client ledger and add client's route again.
Play a firewall: make router2 drop the Fragmentation Needed messages it sends. Then fetch a small page and the 300 KB settlement file from ledger's web server. Predict which one arrives.
Delete the rule, fetch the file again, and ask ledger what it learned about the path back to client.

Last, watch path MTU discovery from client's side with a 1,500-byte ping that has Don't Fragment set (-M do), a 1,400-byte one, and tracepath, which finds the path MTU hop by hop. Stop the network when you're done: docker compose -f env/net.yml down.

With the rule in place, the small page arrives and the big file doesn't: curl got the headers (it knows the file is 300,000 bytes) and not one byte of the body. refs.title: RFC 4821: Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery (TCP)
AWS: Network MTU for EC2 instances (path MTU discovery and ICMP)

analogy: Routing is a chain of sorting offices that each know only their own wall of pigeonholes. A sorter reads the postcode, finds the most specific pigeonhole that fits ("SW1A 1" before "SW1" before "anywhere else: the national hub"), drops the letter in the van for that hole and forgets it. Every envelope also carries a counter that each office ticks down, and a letter whose counter hits zero is thrown away with a short note to the sender: "died at the Croydon office". Traceroute is posting letters with counters of 1, 2, 3 and collecting the notes. The analogy breaks in two places: a real office returns the whole dead letter, while ICMP quotes only its first few dozen bytes, and plenty of internet routers throw letters away without writing any note at all.
world: Your settlement service in an AWS VPC uploads its nightly file to an acquiring bank over a site-to-site VPN. Authorization calls over the same tunnel work all day, because they fit in small packets. The 40 MB settlement upload opens its connection and then hangs until the read timeout. That is a PMTU black hole. The tunnel carries smaller packets than the 1,500 bytes your hosts send, because IPsec adds its own headers to every packet, and somewhere a network ACL or a bank firewall drops ICMP Fragmentation Needed. AWS's MTU page says traffic over a VPN is limited to 1,500 bytes even where instances use 9,001-byte jumbo frames inside the VPC, and warns that a network ACL that denies ICMP breaks path MTU discovery. Before you raise timeouts, run ping -M do -s 1472 and tracepath toward the bank from the same subnet. Ask for ICMP type 3 code 4 to be allowed, or have the VPN router clamp the MSS. Traceroute from a pod that shows stars in the middle of the path is not a finding; stars all the way to the end, with TCP failing too, is.
mistake: The common mistake is blocking all ICMP "for security". It feels safe because ping and traceroute are the only visible casualties. The real casualty is path MTU discovery: once Fragmentation Needed (type 3, code 4) can't get through, every connection whose path has a link smaller than its packets hangs after the handshake, and nothing in any log says why. The same rule shows up in security groups, network ACLs, host firewalls and corporate firewalls in front of partners. Allow at least ICMP type 3 (all codes) and type 11 in both directions, rate-limit them if you must, and clamp the TCP MSS on routers in front of tunnels.

worked.title: Read an ICMP Time Exceeded by hand

steps.say: This is the answer to traceroute's second probe, captured on client: 102 bytes. The first 14 are Ethernet, and the outer IPv4 header starts at byte 14 with 45: version 4, a 20-byte header. Its protocol byte (offset 23) is 01, ICMP. Its source is router2.
steps.code:
0x0000:  1a77 a5ab e1c1 7a2a 923c d76b 0800 45c0
0x0010:  0058 2cd1 0000 3f01 35f4 0a0a 0303 0a0a
0x0020:  010a 0b00 840c 0000 0000 4500 003c 414f

3f          TTL 63: router2 started at 64, router lowered it on the way back
01          protocol 1: ICMP
0a0a 0303   source 10.10.3.3, router2's tunnel side
0a0a 010a   destination 10.10.1.10, client

steps.say: ICMP starts at 14 + 20 = 34. The first byte is the type, then the code, the checksum, and 4 bytes that are unused for this type (Fragmentation Needed puts the MTU in the last two of them).
steps.code:
0b          type 11: time exceeded
00          code 0: TTL ran out in transit
840c        checksum
0000 0000   unused

steps.say: From byte 42 the message quotes the probe as router2 received it. Another IPv4 header, 20 bytes again. Its TTL is 1: the probe left client with 2, and router lowered it.
steps.code:
0x0020:  ...                 4500 003c 414f
0x0030:  0000 0111 5f1d 0a0a 010a 0a0a 0428 dfab

45          quoted IPv4 header, 20 bytes
01          TTL 1 when it reached router2
11          protocol 17: UDP
0a0a 010a   source 10.10.1.10
0a0a 0428   destination 10.10.4.40, ledger

steps.say: The quoted UDP header starts at 42 + 20 = 62: source port, then destination port. 829b is 33435, the port of the second probe. That number is how traceroute knows this answer belongs to TTL 2, and the lab's IcmpReport.parse makes the same walk.
steps.code:
0x0030:  ...                               dfab
0x0040:  829b 0028 197f 4041 ...

dfab        source port 57259 (the kernel's choice)
829b        destination port 33435 = 33434 + (2 - 1): probe 2
0028        UDP length 40: 8 bytes of header, 32 of data

lab.title: A router, a routing table and traceroute
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 28 fail. Ip.kt, Packet.kt and Network.kt are finished: Network passes packets between Nodes and makes hosts answer pings and closed UDP ports. The tests build the lab network in src/test/kotlin/sfz/net/l04/LabNetwork.kt, with the routes the Try its added.
In RoutingTable.kt, write lookup: longest-prefix match in two lines.

In Router.kt, write Node.handle, the router loop from its KDoc: deliver, drop, TTL, route, MTU, forward. Write a private helper that builds the ICMP error, so the two rules about when not to send one live in one place.
In Traceroute.kt, write traceroute. It knows nothing about the network: it hands each probe to send and gets back whatever answered, like a socket would.
In IcmpReport.kt, write parse, the walk from the worked example. The tests feed it four real frames captured in the lab network. Run the tests until all 28 pass.
hints: routes.filter { dst in it.prefix }.maxByOrNull { it.prefix.length } is all of lookup.
Check owns(packet.dst) before the TTL: a packet for the router itself is delivered even with TTL 1. Check the TTL before the route lookup, as Linux does.
The error's source is addressToward(about.src). It quotes about exactly as it arrived, before any TTL change.
In traceroute, accept an answer only if (answer?.body as? IcmpError)?.original?.body is a Udp whose dstPort is this probe's port. Then stop when its type is Icmp.DEST_UNREACHABLE.
In parse, the outer header length is (frame[14].toInt() and 0x0f) * 4. Use ByteBuffer.wrap(frame).getInt(offset) for addresses and getShort(offset).toInt() and 0xffff for ports and the MTU.

drill.title: Predict three traceroutes
drill.prompt: No tools. The path is client (10.10.1.10) to router (10.10.1.2 toward client) to router2 (10.10.3.3 toward client) to ledger (10.10.4.40). Write the hop lines traceroute prints in each case, and name the ICMP type and code behind each line that has an address. (a) Everything works. (b) router2 filters all the ICMP it would send. (c) ledger loses its default route.

answer.html:
(a)  1  10.10.1.2    time exceeded (11/0): TTL 1 died at router
     2  10.10.3.3    time exceeded (11/0): TTL 2 died at router2
     3  10.10.4.40   port unreachable (3/3): the destination answered, stop

(b)  1  10.10.1.2    time exceeded (11/0)
     2  * * *        router2 dropped probe 2 and said nothing
     3  10.10.4.40   port unreachable (3/3): probe 3 got through router2

(c)  1  10.10.1.2    time exceeded (11/0)
     2  10.10.3.3    time exceeded (11/0)
     3  * * *        ledger gets probe 3 but can't route its answer back
     ... * * * until hop 30: it looks exactly like ledger being down

recap: Every router forwards each packet alone: it looks up the destination, picks the next hop and forgets the packet. Of all matching routes, the longest prefix wins.
TTL starts at 64 on Linux and drops by one per router. A router that gets TTL 1 drops the packet and sends ICMP Time Exceeded (type 11) from its address on the way back to you.
Traceroute sends UDP probes to ports 33434 and up with TTL 1, 2, 3 and collects the Time Exceeded messages. The destination's Port Unreachable (3/3) ends the trace.
* * * means no answer came back: filtered or rate-limited ICMP, a real loss, or no route back. Stars in the middle with answers after them say nothing about loss.
Path MTU discovery needs ICMP Fragmentation Needed (3/4) to reach the sender. Block it and you get a black hole: the handshake works, full-size packets vanish and the connection hangs.

explain.prompt: A colleague's traceroute to a partner API shows * * * at hops 5 and 6, then answers at hops 7 to 11. They want to open a ticket about hops 5 and 6. Explain how traceroute works and what those lines do and don't tell you.
explain.answer: Traceroute sends probes with TTL 1, 2, 3 and so on. Each router lowers the TTL, and the router that gets a probe with TTL 1 drops it and sends back ICMP Time Exceeded from its own address, so each line is the router where one probe died. The destination answers with Port Unreachable, which ends the trace. A star only means no ICMP answer came back for that probe. Hops 7 to 11 answering proves the probes for those TTLs went through hops 5 and 6, so those routers forward fine. They just don't send ICMP to us, because they filter it or rate-limit it. That's no reason for a ticket. If the API is slow, look at the hop where the latency jumps and stays high to the end, or at stars that continue to the very end while TCP fails too.

deeper.html:
Where traceroute lies. Big networks spread traffic over several equal routes (ECMP, equal-cost multipath), usually by hashing each packet's addresses and ports. Classic traceroute changes the destination port for every probe, so each probe may take a different branch, and a trace can show hops that are never on one real path. Paris traceroute keeps the fields the routers hash on constant so that all probes follow one path; Linux's traceroute has -U and -T modes that fix the port. Tunnels such as MPLS can also hide whole stretches of routers, which then never touch the TTL.

ICMP redirects. In the first traceroute Try it, router received packets from client and sent them back out of the same card, to Docker's gateway. A Linux router in that position sends client an ICMP Redirect (type 5): "next time, send these straight to 10.10.1.1". Client ignores it, because containers have net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0, which is also the safe setting for servers.

Anycast. 1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8 are announced in BGP from hundreds of places at once, and longest-prefix match plus BGP's own path choice send you to the nearest one. That is why a traceroute to 1.1.1.1 ends after a handful of hops wherever you are, and why the same address answers from a different city on another network.

IPv6. The IPv6 header calls the TTL the hop limit, and ICMPv6 has its own numbers: Time Exceeded is type 3 and Packet Too Big, the IPv6 version of Fragmentation Needed, is type 2. IPv6 routers never fragment, so blocking Packet Too Big breaks IPv6 even harder than blocking 3/4 breaks IPv4.
